utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Sarah Clanton, legal intern Mirko Roguljic, and case manager Thomas Laugel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell, with case manager Negosava Smiljanic, and intern Milan Jovancevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. We have a short oral ruling. On the 3rd of July, 2014, the Defence request to replace translation of D00021 was filed. The Defence requests that the current English translation of D21 be replaced with a corrected version provided by CLSS. Is the Prosecution in a position to make submissions in this respect?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm 95 per cent sure that there's no objection to that but I just -- if I could take one moment to double-check to make sure that I've got the same document in mind that the Chamber does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: One moment or after the first break, what --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, the first break. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks. Good morning, Mr. Hadzic. I remind you that you're still under oath. Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, first of all, I wanted to put some questions to you about the Serbian National Council that was mentioned several times here. So can you tell us when this Serbian National Council was established in the first place, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Croatia, the Serbian National Council was established in 1990 in Srb. I mean for all of Croatia, that all-Croatian one. But the regional one was established on the 7th of January, 1991. That's the one that is discussed the most over here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the reason was for establishing the regional Serbian National Council, that is to say, for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb people expressed their views through the Serb Democratic Party. Most of the people who worked with me and also Koncarevic and Petrovic thought that some super-party body should be established consisting of people who are not members of the SDS but who are Serbs who live in the territory of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So what was the function of this Serbian National Council supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To express the will of the Serb -- of the people living there, primarily the Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the time when the Serbian National Council was established, do you remember whether the Croatian authorities had already started the arming that had to do with members of the HDZ?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that even before the Serbian National Council was established, that is to say, before the new year, in autumn and winter of 1990, we had a lot of information about the arming of Croats. Actually, their Serb neighbours saw them being armed with long-barrelled weapons, and this caused panic among the Serb people, so we had information about the Croats arming themselves. When I say "Croats," I mean members of the HDZ because this was arming along party lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have -- or, rather, did you have any direct or indirect knowledge about the arming that was taking place?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, basically I had direct information, almost 99 per cent. I did not see that, but people who came to see me had seen that personally. And I personally saw people in the street, reserve policemen, with weapons. There were that's well-known incidents around Osijek, in bars. When one of Vladimir Glavas's men quarrelled with people because of music in a tavern, then they'd go home and they'd get more people with automatic weapons, and that was a terrible thing, that people could resort to automatic weapons because of some kind of quarrel in a tavern.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P1762.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do we have a problem, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It is P1762.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You had an opportunity to read this document. So, tell me: When you spoke about the establishment of this main Serbian National Council in 1990, is this a piece of news that was carried with regard to its establishment?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is that news or, rather, the decision of the SNS to declare a referendum. I mean, the one established in Srb. And I was not a member of that. There were almost 100.000 Serbs there, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me whether there was any link and, if so, what was that link like, between the Serb National Council that was established in Knin, the one that we're talking about now, and the regional council that was established for Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no practical link. In a way, there was a formal link, although all of that was within Croatia. These were two completely independent councils.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, it -- it's already admitted. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Zivanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The Serb National Council, on the 26th of February, 1991, passed a declaration on sovereign autonomy of the Serb people of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, P81.50.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I remember that declaration, but I was made aware of it later. In February, I didn't really attach any importance to it. I didn't even know what it represented, and I did not take part in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that you did not take part in it, does that mean that you did not draft this declaration?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that, but it also means that I don't know who wrote it. To this day, I don't know who wrote it. Because they had not consulted me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sometime after the establishment of the Serb National Council, do you remember that an order was made by the Presidency of the SFRY to disband all armed formations that were not within the single armed forces of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D2186.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember, yes. That was carried by all the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember whether this order was carried out in Croatia? Do you remember whether, after that, some formations were disarmed, formations of the HDZ and other formations, that were not established in accordance with these requirements from the order of the Presidency of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course not. Of course, it wasn't carried out in Croatia. This order, in a way, just quieted people a bit and we relaxed a bit, and we thought that the federal state would resolve problems through its own instruments. However, it was not resolved, and according to the information I have, no attempt was even made.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D112, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the first two days of your testimony, you mentioned twice, or, rather, even more than that, you mentioned that you were shocked by the film that you saw on television. In it, the then-minister of defence of Croatia, Martin Spegelj, spoke about the arming of the HDZ and their supporters and the possible killing of their opponents. I would just like us to take a look at a few excerpts from this video.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It is P1200. We shall see portion from 41 second, to 1 minute and 20 seconds. In B/C/S -- in English transcript, this text is on the page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, tell me whether this video is what you spoke about when you testified about the fear that it caused among other Serbs, yourself included, after having seen it on television?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is that video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I didn't hear any translation of what was said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It -- this video is admitted into evidence and there is a transcript in English. It is P1200.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not have that transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can replay it, it is very short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let's do that, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the translation; hence, we are not in a position to interpret. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Do we had it on the screen now? Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, I suggest that you provide this transcript to the interpreters and that we play the video again after the break. Because this doesn't work. We can't follow the testimony without knowing what has been said.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: That's okay, Your Honour. We'll do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We will show the video later and then I will put you -- my questions related to the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we now see 1D2189, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, it would be helpful that you mention the tab number of the documents you are asking on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is no -- there is no date in this particular document, but in the next -- in the text on next page -- on this page, on the right side of the page, it is March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: March 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Zivanovic. It's not the date I'm asking for. It's the tab number of your document list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tab number ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Yeah. Your document list has -- let's see. The first column of your document list gives tabs numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh, you don't have them on the document you have there. Because the -- I don't know whether it was the previous one or the one before, I couldn't find with the -- with the 65 ter number. So it would be helpful to have the tab numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: We'll get back to this document later. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, go ahead. Go ahead. Go ahead. But next document, if you could, please add the tab number as well so that we can check. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the text? Do you remember this appeal by the then-president of the municipality, Slavko Dokmanovic, that appeal was read on Radio Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember. I did not listen to it on Radio Vukovar but then it was published in a newspaper.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What prompted this appeal, what kind of a situation?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The news on the arming of the HDZ caused panic among the Serbian population. People were in panic, and they started sending their wives and children to Serbia in an unorganised manner, spontaneously, because they were afraid that the Croats would attack the Serbian villages where they lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, tab number is 1022.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D113, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you mentioned that after you were released from prison, after the developments in Plitvice, you visited the American ambassador in Belgrade, Mr. Zimmermann. Do you remember when that happened?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that event very clearly. I knew even before I saw this document that it was in mid-April but now I see that it was on the 12th of April. I remember that event very well. Although I do have a bit of amnesia for everything that happened a month after my arrest, but that was the biggest thing that could ever happen to me, meeting with the American ambassador in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see 1D2181. It is tab 1410. May we see the second page of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Under 3, somewhere in the middle of the document, it says that at the request of the president of the Serbian Democratic Party, Dr. Raskovic, the ambassador and the political advisor received you on the 12th of April and that Ilija Sasic and Veljko Dzakula accompanied you. Do you remember that the two of them were also present at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that there were the three of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now you can see what problems you presented to the ambassador, a description of the situation in your region. It says here, amongst other things, that almost all ethnic Serbs have been fired from official jobs, especially in the courts, prosecutor's offices, and the police. Is it true that you presented that situation to the ambassador?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we said that, and it was a fact. I have to emphasise that Sasic and Dzakula had been well prepared for that meeting, and they had checked everything. I arrived there after that incident. I thought I was there as a case in point, as a person who had been a victim of the situation. So they were talking much more than I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It also says here that a condition on landing a job at the Croatian police was not only the ethnic affiliation to the Croatian people but also the membership in the HDZ. Is this a true reflection of what was going on in Croatia at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here as well that a majority of the Serbian teachers were fired and that the curricula concerning Serbian history and culture had been changed or altered. Did you also say that to the ambassador?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what they said, because that's how things were.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the paragraph preceding bullet point 4, it says that all three of you said that the beatings of Serbs by the Croatian police or civilians and other physical abuse was becoming a daily matter. And also that barricades and armed patrols on both sides had become the norm. Did you, indeed, say that to the American ambassador at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we said that. Unfortunately, it was the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since you do not have the Serbian translation of this document, I'm going to read paragraph 4 to you, which speaks about you precisely. It says here: [In English] "Goran Hadzic is one of the SDP leaders detained by the Croatian police at Plitvice on March 31st. He was obviously still very badly shaken by the arrest and by what he described as a severe beating he received from the police. Hadzic insisted that the SDP leaders who met at Plitvice were not discussing a revolt against Croatia or any kind of armed action or uprising. On the contrary, he said, the people in the meeting were moderates who were discussing ways in which to establish some kind of constructive dialogue with the Croatian authorities. With considerable bitterness he added that if the police had microphones in the room, they would know that -- this." [Interpretation] Tell me, please, does this truly reflect your own situation and what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is 100 per cent as I said it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And now I'm going to ask you to look at paragraph 5, which reads: [In English] "The SDP leaders indicated that they and Serbs in eastern Croatia do not entirely share the views of Milan Babic and his Knin Serbs in the so-called Serbian Autonomous Province of Krajina. The Slavonia/Baranja Serbs, they said, have not joined the Krajina Serbs in seceding from Croatia and do not see secession as the only desirable or acceptable solution. They stated several times that they are prepared to continue to live in Croatia, but only a democratic Croatia within a Yugoslav Federation. It is only such structure, they said, which can guarantee them protection and respect for their national rights." [Interpretation] Did you discuss this? Do you remember? Was it said that you did not share the views of Babic and his people from Knin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was said at the meeting, and this only confirmed the situation that it was. It was a matter of general knowledge that we were not in agreement with Babic, but when I look at the English translation, I can see the SDP, but it is the SDS. There is the SDP party, but this party is not the SDP but the SDS, Serbian Democratic Party. So there is a -- a mistake in the English version of the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the English abbreviation for the SDS because the words "stranka" which means "party" in English, starts with a P?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I know that there was a party in Croatia known as the SDP. So I just wanted to make sure that the difference is noted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further on it says: [In English] "They specifically mentioned the Yugoslav People's Army, JNA, as an institution which protected their rights, but they added that they have been disappointed with the JNA's action recently, particularly in Pakrac and Plitvice. The army, they said, should act quickly to prevent interethnic violence and confrontation in the first place, and not simply step in when the victims have already fallen. Because of what they perceive as the JNA's tardy and inadequate response [sic] to the Pakrac and Plitvice situation, Serbs, they said, are increasingly relying on themselves for self-defence." [Interpretation] Tell me, please, when it comes to your protection by the JNA, did you also present that to the ambassador?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is what we said at the time. This reflected the situation as it was on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ... you see towards the end of this last paragraph, page 5, we see: [In English] "When asked whether they are satisfied with the support they are getting from Belgrade and Serbia, President Milosevic, the SDP leaders were surprisingly non-committal. They stressed that they do not take orders or instructions from Belgrade and they clearly implied that Babic and the Krajina Serbs do and also indicated some fear that their interests would be sold out in a Milosevic/Tudjman deal. Regardless of what the two republic presidents agree on, they said, they act in response to their conditions locally and will defend their own interests." [Interpretation] Tell me, do you remember whether this was said at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember. We said it that way, and that was the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, since I can't see it in this report, what did the American ambassador tell you, or maybe his advisor who accompanied him?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps I should first tell you the reason why we went there, from my perspective. To present the problem - that was the first reason - and the second reason was to gain some knowledge to arrive at a proposal for a solution. Then, as now, I believed we had come to the highest possible level, considering the territory we came from. The embassy of the largest and most powerful state in the world, and in fact we were seeking the ambassador's opinion. He said, and to us this gave some satisfaction and provided us with some guide-lines in what to do in the future, that his government would not support any separatist republics, or recognise them, and that they would be supporting a united SFRY. To me, that was the key thing. That's what I remember from the whole meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this encouraging news, not only to you but also to the people from your area to whom you conveyed it?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. I couldn't wait to go back and tell everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D114, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, when you said this news was very encouraging to you, these words of the American ambassador, tell me, did you hear any other similar statements to the effect that other countries, too, would support a united SFRY?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was not the only statement of that kind. It was the position of, I would say, the majority of the member states of the then-European Union and the United Nations, but I remember specifically the Italian Prime Minister De Michelis, who said it in so many that words, and it was widely publicised.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we have 1D915. It is tab 808.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see in this text that he also talked about the right to self-determination. Have you read this? Maybe it's too small to read from the screen, but I have a hard copy with larger print.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've read it, that he supports the rights of people to self-determination, and he says specifically "including the Serbian people."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you understand this statement he made? How did you understand his position?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can speak in my own name and in the name of people to whom I personally talked. I understood that as them supporting our position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D115, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Last time we left off on the subject of your meetings with Boljkovac and Degoricija after the events at Plitvice, sometime in April 1991. You said he travelled to Vukovar very often. That's on pages 94 to 99 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D2192. 2192, sorry. 1D.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can see the text published in the newspaper of the Vukovar municipality. Can you tell us, was this one of the meetings that you mentioned as having been designed as a way to defuse the situation in Vukovar municipality?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's one of these meetings. We had meetings of that kind every week and even more often. This one was just at a higher level because Boljkovac came along with Degoricija. Before that, Degoricija came alone, before the situation got more complicated. I remember that meeting. I was one of the participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was discussed at the meeting? Were there any specific conclusions? Was something specific done?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As this newspaper story says, the purpose of the meeting was to diffuse tensions, as we called it at the time. There were no particularly conclusions except that Mr. Boljkovac and Mr. Degoricija gave verbal promises that the situation would calm down there so there was no reason for concern, but obviously these were just words, and the Serbs were not happy. And in a way, despite these guarantees, they were wondering why we are not happy, and I remember there were some problems about that. There was Rade Leskovac as well, from Vera village, at that meeting. That was the first time I met him. He made a very unusual digression and made a comment - I don't know if I mentioned this before - he said it would be unusual for one person to walk naked around town, but if you see 1.000 of them doing that, then you should wonder what the reason is. In the same way, you should not be surprised that we Serbs are afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says in the text that before coming to this meeting, Degoricija and Boljkovac had a meeting with Radmilo Bogdanovic in Backa Palanka. Tell me, were there any direct meetings between the highest leaders of Serbia, on one hand, and Croatia on the other? Were there any media reports about that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were. And that's how we learned about these meetings. I don't think Boljkovac ever told us at that meeting that he seen Radmilo Bogdanovic. I think I read it in the newspaper. But I'm not 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you were released from prison after Plitvice - I believe it was on the 3rd of April - and when you came back to Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem, you saw the barricades. What happened later with these barricades? Did they remain standing or were there any changes?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After Boro Savic and I came back from Plitvice, there was no longer any reason to keep the barricades. They had been set up because we were arrested, and they were removed after we were released. That was the condition for their removal. And Degoricija demanded when releasing me from prison that the barricades be removed, and I succeeded in having them removed. I mean, all of us succeeded. I believe Veljko Dzakula also came one evening to Borovo Selo. But as soon as we removed the barricades, there was some provocation from the Croatian side, and then they are set up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So what was your role in all of that? Did you influence people - and in what way - to have the barricades removed?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was wholeheartedly trying to have the barricades removed. I had no question in my mind it should be done, and most of the people I knew shared the same view. Nobody enjoyed sleeping at the barricades and keeping them at any cost. In my understanding, barricades were a type of defence, and if it turns out there's nothing to fear, then barricades are not needed. I trusted Mr. Degoricija and Boljkovac, of course, and I thought there was nothing to fear, and the barricades should be removed. I didn't have any special authority so that people should listen to me, but most people thought the same way I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we have D5. It is tab 1223.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will show you a couple of passages from the book of Josip Boljkovac that was published much later in 2009. He is reminiscing about these events and the time when he was the minister of the interior of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see B/C/S page 5. It is English page 26. It seems it is ... we should go to B/C/S -- B/C/S chapter 47. Sorry, I have wrong page here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you see this, this page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we go to next page in B/C/S, please. And next one. That's it. And just to find it in English, it might be 27. Maybe 28. 29, please. 30, if we can. Yeah, that's here. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you will see here is that the provocations that were characteristic of Serb extremists in the area of the Krajina municipalities, it says then were matched by what happened in Slovenia and often there were incidents on the ground, and, according to the information I had then, were mostly provoked by the Croatian side. Tell me, please, this information, does it correspond to the knowledge that you had at the time?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 100 per cent. When the Croatian minister admitted that they had provoked -- well, they say it was mostly the Croatian side that was actually provoking, doing the provoking, but he didn't want to be too harsh by saying it was 100 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now take a look at the next paragraph that has to do with things that happened in the second half of March 1991.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He made a mistake there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I see that you know what incident this is about, so can you tell us what it was that had actually happened and when. If you say that he made a mistake, tell us what the mistake is?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mid-April. He got the wrong month. As I've already said, when Boro and I returned from Plitvice, both Boro and I and the entire leadership of the SDS advocated the removal of the barricades, and barricades were removed everywhere. Traffic was normalised throughout Eastern Slavonia and Baranja. However, obviously this did not suit someone in Zagreb. And in mid-April, I think in the second half of April, somebody fired three shells at Borovo Selo. When I say "somebody," well, I, at the time, did not know who it was. That's why I'm saying "somebody." It's only now from this book that I see who it was that had fired that. And I remember that event very well because I barely survived. I advocated the removal of barricades. I went all over the village. I was telling people in the street that there was no problem whatsoever, that I reached an agreement with the Croatian authorities, and they started shooting at the village then. And then this woman in front of whose house that shell fell, I really don't know how I managed to get away then without being lynched by the people there. As she said, the shell fell where she had been standing with her two children, and then she entered the house, and then the shell fell right there on that path where they had been standing five minutes before that. And now I'm thinking about this. These children, had they been killed then, then the people would have killed me. I would have had no way of surviving, and I was the one who was in favour of the removal of barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In this text, he identified people who did that, and he said what his source of this information was. In your assessment, this source that provided this information that is noted here, was this a reliable source?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to take a look at this first to see what his source is. Yes, yes, 100 per cent reliable source because I personally knew Mr. Kir, and he was along the same lines as the leadership of Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem. However, his fate was worse than mine. They just beat me up, but they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that he was on the same positions, can you define this a bit? Can you tell us in what way? He was not a member of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. Well, we were not of the same ethnicity, so, in a way, we were on two sides ethnically, but our position was the same in view of resolving the problem. We wanted to have problems resolved by way of negotiations. I don't know. I don't want to say anything that would not be right, but Mr. Kir probably was one of the most sincere Croats I knew, and he really wanted to resolve problems by peaceful means. I'm not saying that there weren't other sincere people there at the time, but Mr. Kir figured prominently in that respect. In his heart and soul.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we see, please, 1D271.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Tab number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. It is tab 738.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, can you tell us whether you know who compiled this document, this text?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the title shows that this is a document of the joint council of municipalities from Vukovar, Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So I see that this was compiled considerably after the war.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, 2001. So this institution is a Serb institution but within the Croatian state. So it's a Croatian institution and the members are Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you take a look at page 3 or, rather, page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Before counsel continues, I'd like to object to this procedure. This document is not in evidence as far as I know. It is some sort of compilation prepared by Serbs in Croatia who we don't know. Whether it is purporting to be in the nature of some expert report or some historical summary from a point of view that was prepared some ten years after the conflict. But, in any event, I think to put the document in front of the witness, not knowing anything about it and simply to have the witness hold forth, if you will, as to his views and comments on it is not appropriate. Let counsel ask the witness a question, and let the witness answer. But the document itself is not appropriate to use as some springboard for the client -- for the witness to say yes or no, I agree with this or not. So we object to the procedure on those grounds. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, do you have a reply to the objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I shall put to the witness some questions related to this document and then show him it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Let's first hear the questions, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you know that sometime at the end of March 1991, in Bogdanovci, the first public lineup of armed Croatian civilians took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I object to the leading question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you know, Mr. Hadzic, that at any point in time, in any place, Croats were lined up, armed Croats?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us something about what you know.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first I learned of this was from my associates, that this happened in Bogdanovci. This is a village near Vukovar, but from my village, there are three or four villages before you reach Bogdanovci. It caused anxiety. That's why I found out about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this perhaps portrayed in the media?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that this was portrayed in the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whether, at that time, sometime in the summer of 1991, were there any armed actions?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the Croatian side?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, not only the summer, but it started from Plitvice, the spring. In fact, the end of the winter. And then there was Borovo Selo. And then -- and then later on, it escalated to the blockade of the barracks in Vukovar. That was the summer of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any cases of attacks against citizens of Serb ethnicity before the conflict broke out? So can you remember some names?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a generally known thing. How do I put this? Well, it's not hundreds and hundreds, but there were tens and tens of such cases. Also, some of my acquaintances and even some of my friends were attacked. They were attacked -- it was mostly houses of prominent Serbs that were attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we hear their names perhaps? If necessary, if I think that that is more convenient, we could move into private session. Tell us.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. One name is that of a person who testified here and I'm not sure that this person had protective measures. So perhaps it would be fairer if we were to move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at 1D271.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: On page 5, can you see --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, it is page 4. Page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you see some of the names that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic, that's -- that's the document Mr. Stringer objected to; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I understood that I have to put further question and then to -- to show to the witness the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Well, if there's no objection anymore from Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, the objection stands. Mr. Hadzic has clearly got his own independent recollection of these events. He is recalling names, dates, places in some detail, so again it's unclear why we need to look at a document written by people for whom -- who we don't know about. There's still no foundation for the document itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Because Mr. Hadzic could explain, to see these events, these names, and other details, and to let us know if he knows anything about it, and he could confirm whether these details or these data are correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Then we are back to the first objection -- to Mr. Stringer's first objection, Mr. Zivanovic. I'm afraid I have to sustain his objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, do you remember whether, on the 1st of May, 1991, there were some incidents in Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally participated in calming the situation down after the incident. In Brsadin, which is the neighbouring village, a villager was killed. He was a Serb. It was a custom in the region to mark the 1st of May as the Labour Day. We would get up very early in the morning and rally on that day, to celebrate. It was a custom that had been introduced already during the Communist reign. A citizen, whose family name was Inic, got up. He walked through the village to the neighbouring forest with a state flag in his hands. His neighbour, a Croat, called Gelencir, for no reason at all, killed him just because he was carrying a Yugoslav flag. There had not been a previous history of quarrels or arguments. They were on good terms before that incident. The story continues. I can tell you what happened next and how the day ended. Since this was a neighbouring village, I learnt what had happened. The population of Brsadin were mostly Serbs, 90 per cent of them were Serbs. They tried to lynch the Croat. That would have been not only illegal but totally insane. Milenko Milinkovic was from Brsadin and he was a deputy in the Croatian Parliament. He hailed from Brsadin and had come home for the weekend. Together with me and some other people he prevented that lynching. We called the police from Vinkovci and those people from Brsadin handed over Gelencir to the Vinkovci police. The story continues. I heard that a couple of years ago as I was watching the Croatian television programme. Gelencir's son or daughter, I forget, was a guest on one of the TV shows. She said that he had died but he was never put on trial, and ever since he has been hailed as a hero in Croatia and nobody has posed any problems to the family. This means that justice in that case has never been done. Can I say something about the institution which is mentioned in here? Although the Trial Chamber has rejected document, I don't want to go into that. The institution in question was given to the Serbian people by the European Agreement. It's an institution of the Croatian state. Their letter is not a letter without an address. They are the officials of the Croatian state, and their address, the address of the common council of municipalities, has a full title. They are Serbs who live in Croatia. They are citizens as all the other citizens of Croatia, with equal rights. They were already discriminated once and I don't think that they should be discriminated by anybody, albeit unintentional. Those were not Serbs who supported me. Those were Serbs who supported the Croatian government and the Croatian administration. They lived in Croatia, and this was printed and released by the Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: This was totally unnecessary, Mr. Hadzic. Mr. Zivanovic, would this be an appropriate moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. To inform the Chamber, the Prosecution has no objection to the Defence motion on substituting the translation for D21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Trial Chamber instructs the Registry to replace the English translation of D21 with the corrected transcription now available in e-court. Mr. Zivanovic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Hadzic, could you now tell us, please, what you know about the incident in Borovo Selo on the 2nd of May, 1991.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My knowledge is almost first-hand, but it is certainly second-hand because I was not a participant in the event. I spent a lot of time in Borovo Selo during the war and after the war until the reintegration in 1997. I spoke to a number of the villagers and they told me what had happened. However, I will tell you what my direct knowledge is because this is relevant. Since I was one of the participants in the talks with the Croatian side, on the 2nd of May, 1991, I was at home in the morning. It was a bank holiday, or perhaps it was a Sunday; I don't know. Slavko Degoricija called me on the phone around half past 9.00 or 10.00, or thereabouts. The conversation was informal, almost friendly, I would say. He asked me to try and talk to Vukasin Soskocanin because he knew about our relationship with the aim of removing the barricades in Borovo Selo. They had been re-erected by Susak, Vukojevic, and Glavas after the August incident, as we have just explained.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. I apologise. Could you please repeat the names of the people. Just one name has been recorded and that is the name of Glavas.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gojko Susak, who was the defence minister at the time in Croatia. Vice Vukojevic, who was the assistant minister for the police. And Branimir Glavas. They were the ones who organised the attack. Josip Reihl-Kir was also with them, but he didn't know what was going on. He only brought them to the place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Apologies to counsel. There was one name that I think I was hoping to hear - it might have also been missed - which was the name that Mr. Degoricija asked Mr. Hadzic to contact someone about removing the barricades. And I don't know that that name appeared either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you please repeat the name who was supposed to remove the barricades at Mr. Degoricija's request.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Degoricija asked me to talk to Vukasin Soskocanin, Vukasin. At that time he was the commander of Borovo Selo, the commander of the defence of Borovo Selo, better say. I called Vukasin and I told him what I thought, but Vukasin knew that already. I told him that I was against the barricades. However, after the incident that I had with the population of Borovo Selo, when I advocated the removal of the barricades and Susak opened fire at Borovo Selo, and when people in Borovo Selo attacked me, I couldn't share my position with Vukasin. I just told him what Degoricija's request was. Vukasin and Degoricija knew each other personally, obviously. I knew that there was a problem in Borovo Selo and that people had already had enough of the barricades. Borovo had nearly 10.000 inhabitants, and I believe that about 800 of them were also employees of the Borovo factory. They didn't have any arable land, they didn't have any other source of income. Their only source of income was the salary that they received from the Borovo factory. A majority of them put a pressure on the village staff to remove the barricades because they wanted to go to the factory to get their monies and to avoid being fired. From this perspective now, I can see that Croatia could hardly wait to be put in a position to fire them. Vukasin told me to call Degoricija and to tell him that he as well could not wait for the barricades to be removed and that they would be removed straight away. I called Degoricija and told him that. He thanked me. The conversation was rather polite. He wanted us to see each other some time soon, and so on and so forth. After a while, I drove my daughter to see a doctor at the Vukovar Hospital, along with my wife. In the village, we picked up another two women who were going to Vukovar, to give them a lift. One of them was employed at the agricultural pharmacy in the village, and the other was my daughter's teacher living in Vukovar. At the entrance to Vukovar, near Suma Djergaj, we were stopped by a police patrol. That seemed very unusual to me because there were over 20 policemen in that patrol wearing camouflage uniforms. They asked to see my ID and other documents that I didn't have on me. That policeman then approached his boss and said there was a problem. The other one approached us, looked into my car and recognised my wife. They had been classmates in Nustar. They even shared the same desk. And without even looking at me, he said: Zivka is here. You can let them through. No problem. She's a friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me for stopping you here. Could you just explain why you had no ID on you?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My documents and money and everything had been taken away at Plitvice. I was robbed. Degoricija had promised that they would be returned so I did not apply for new documents. I explained that yesterday. I went to Zagreb and they did not return my documents, and they didn't say anything definitive so I was still hoping that they would find my documents. I was not hoping to get the pistol and the money back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Continue.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was planning to go to the Secretariat of the Interior just after the holidays and apply for new documents. When they let us through, it was a couple of hundred metres before the junction where you go left to Vukovar and to the right for Borovo Naselje. The other way around: Vukovar is to the right, and Borovo Naselje to the left. [In English] Yes. [Interpretation] And I saw a motorcade of police cars passing by in great haste. I had to stop and let them pass. I didn't suspect anything. I thought there had been an accident or something. At the hospital, my wife and daughter got out. Perhaps it's interesting to note that they were going to see Dr. Vesna Bosanac. She was the attending physician for my children. And I continued to the centre of the city to drop off these two ladies. On my way back, I was recognised by a former classmate at the market-place, Branko Ponjevic [phoen]. Ponjevic, Ponjevic. P as Paris. He suddenly made a U-turn on the road, with the tires squealing, and shouted at the top of his voice, almost crying: They had attacked Borovo Selo, curse their mothers. My children are just now in Borovo Selo spending the weekend at their grandparents. Branko was a traffic policeman in Vukovar before the war. I got into my car quickly and went to the municipal building in Vukovar to see Slavko Dokmanovic, president of the municipality. However, Slavko was not there. There was only his secretary, and she was in tears. She told me that Slavko had gone to the barracks to see the commander of the barracks. I understood only then that I could get in trouble again the way I had at Plitvice, especially since I no longer had any documents. I drove quickly to the hospital where my family was already waiting outside because they had heard what had happened, and the police was already surrounding the hospital; the Croatian police, I mean. I went to hide at my relatives who lived close to the hospital, and I stayed there for five or six days until I camouflaged myself. That means shaving off my beard, putting on a cap, and crossing the Danube in a boat. On the Serbian side of the Danube, there were already a lot of cars, the cars belonging to local residents of the places alongside Dunav who volunteered to give a ride to the refugees and take them to Serbia. We were taken across by one resident of Backa Novo Selo, I believe, whose name was Sead. His nickname was Sejo. He was a Muslim. I became friends with him, you can say. We met quite a few times after the war. I crossed the Danube from Borovo Selo by boat, and then went by boat back again to get my son, who was four years old. He had stayed in Pacetin. And my then-wife and daughter were taken to Kljajicevo village as refugees. At that time, the telephones were still working so I was able to get a call through to Pacetin, and somebody brought my sister, Goranka, and my son to Borovo Selo. And then I took them to Kljajicevo to join my wife and daughter. That's what happened to me from the 7th of May onwards. I was a direct participant in these events, and my knowledge about the events of the 2nd May that are 99 per cent accurate are briefly as follows. Very soon after my conversation with Degoricija, perhaps just an hour or 90 minutes later, around half past 11.00, the barricades were removed. And then around noon, or perhaps 12.15, the Croatian police entered Borovo Selo from the side of Borovo Naselje with two or three vehicles and two or three buses -- and two buses. I -- those were the vehicles I had seen at that junction when I was taking a turn to Vukovar. As soon as they came in, they fell to the ground at the canal and started shooting. In the centre, they killed a guard who stood outside the local commune building. His last name was Milic and he was a volunteer. He was just sitting there, unarmed. His rifle was lying on the ground 50 metres away from him. And they wounded another local resident. That rifle was about 10 metres away from the guard, not 50. And they were shouting at Vukasin Soskocanin that he should surrender, and then they ran into the building of the local commune. But there was no one up there on the first floor. The leader of that group was called Stipo Bosnjak. He entered the building, and on the ground floor there was an outpatient clinic or an infirmary. It was full of people, mostly children. When I say "people," I mean women, women and children. And he took a child and used it as a life shield. It was perhaps 30 minutes into their raid. During those first 30 minutes, nobody responded to their fire. Nobody returned fire because nobody was expecting that attack. Later on, the clashes got worse and, according to official data, 12 Croatian policemen were killed and one Serb, this man Milic, and more Serbs were wounded. That group that was coming to Borovo Selo from Osijek was not very well synchronised and they were late, so that people from that part of Borovo Selo hearing the shooting put up the barricades again and didn't let them in. Then the Yugoslav People's Army arrived and escorted safely all the Croatian policemen out. This is what I know, briefly, although I've heard many more details. Perhaps it's interesting to note that at the outskirts of the village, Croatian policemen entered a cafe that was located in a basement. The cafe was called San Marino. And there, they took about 20 young people hostages, young girls and boys. Some friends of mine were there as well and later on we called him "Hostage," in jest. Well, that would be it, briefly. However, the Croatian media tried to portray this as an ambush. Since I was a direct participant in the talks with Degoricija, I can say here before you with 100 per cent certainty that it was not an ambush. This very fact that I went to hospital with my child, that the infirmary in Borovo Selo was full of children, and that the cafe was full of young people, all of that shows that there was no ambush there whatever. Also, later on, some say that the fire was returned by the locals of Borovo Selo 30 minutes later, on hour and a half later. And now these stories that some people have been telling, people from Serbia, leaders, saying that their volunteers took part in this, this was exaggerated. Because there was this group of volunteers of the Serb Radical Party in Borovo Selo - there were very few of them, actually, there weren't more than six of them then, on the 2nd of May - when the barricades were removed around 11.00, they returned their weapons and they planned to cross the Danube. So, at first, they could not even respond to gun-fire. But I found out about all of that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, you said that at the end of this conflict the JNA entered Borovo Selo. Tell us, to the best of your knowledge, did the JNA withdraw after that from Borovo Selo or did they stay there?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to the best of my knowledge and on the basis of fact -- of factual evidence, they stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain the following to us now. Since you went to Serbia with your family and you told us that you first stayed in the village of Kljajicevo, where did you go after that? How long did your family stay in Kljajicevo and where did they stay after that?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They stayed in Kljajicevo very briefly. I mean, I cannot say exactly right now. And they were transferred as refugees to stay with a family in Backa Palanka. Since I could not get my car across the Danube, we had a problem, a transportation problem. When I borrow somebody's car, then I cannot really drive because I did not have any documents. Not only documents for driving but also documents for identification. When we arrived Backa Palanka, I tried to get some documents at the Backa Palanka SUP. However, they could not give me any. They told me to wait until the situation was normalised with Vukovar or otherwise I would have to take a driving test again. That was insane for me to pay for all of that. I could not go to driving school again and pay for that and the exam. Then I tried to find some connections, trying to sidestep all of this --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing: Can you tell us how long you stayed in Backa Palanka with your family? Tell us whether you changed your place of residence.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. I haven't given a full answer about that. Well, towards the end of August, or almost the beginning of September, we went to Novi Sad. It was an apartment for refugees. It was not a very good apartment but at least we were on our own. It was a room -- it was an apartment consisting of one room and another smaller room. And also the roof was flat and it was leaking, but that was better than nothing. I know that my daughter started school, second grade it was. That was in Novi Sad. So, on the 10th of September, we were in Novi Sad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Who was staying in this apartment that consisted of one room and another smaller room, as you said?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My wife, two children, I, and my sister.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us how it was that you found out about the death of Vukasin Soskocanin.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was by chance that I was on the Danube on the 15th of May. As I said a moment ago, when I went to the police station in Backa Palanka to get documents, that was technically impossible. I was trying to find some connections. I even went to see the president of the municipality, Ljubo Novakovic, and he said that he couldn't do anything. I knew the police commander. I think his last name was Cavka and his first name was Lazar, Lazo. He couldn't do anything either. And then I bumped in Lazo Sarac who worked for state security of Serbia in Backa Palanka. That's what I learned. I indicated what my problem was to everyone, and I said that I had to go to Pacetin to see what the situation was. I didn't know what was going on in my village. Then Lazo said that he was planning -- well, you see, we saw each other on the 14th and he was planning to go to Borovo Selo on the following day and he could help me get across. We could go together because I could not find that place where the boat would cross the river. That was quite complicated. I wasn't a local person there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I do apologise to you now. I see that you mentioned some names here. I planned for us to do that in private session. My only question to you was whether you were on the Danube when you learned -- actually how was it that you learned about Soskocanin's death?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do apologise. I thought that I was supposed to explain how it was that I got there. Yes, I was on the Danube. Perhaps I arrived an hour or two -- well, all of this was a bit -- a bit confusing for me. Perhaps an hour or two after he drowned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what it was that you heard then? What was this information that you had about that, about how Vukasin Soskocanin lost his life?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about that from the horse's mouth. I came across all these people who were on the Danube when all of that had happened. And later on, I talked to the people who were on the same boat with Vukasin who survived. There was even an elderly woman there who had originally hailed from Pacetin and who married in Borovo Selo, so I talked to her too. There were six of them on that boat: Vukasin, his two friends or escorts or perhaps friends, then that woman, and then the man who was in charge of the boat, and then these two other people from Borovo Selo. A Bulgarian ship came along, as these people who lived by the Danube say and they are more familiar with the river than I am. This was a very heavy ship, and it's not like a normal ship. It creates a different kind of waves. They were perhaps 50 metres to 100 metres from the place that they had set out to -- or, rather, where they had started from, and they were about 20 metres away from the bank of the river, but the bank is different there. I mean, there's no shallow water. You get into deep water immediately. When the first wave hit them, the boat was still on the surface. There was water in the boat but it hadn't sunk completely. Vukasin got up and he said to them: Don't be scared. Everything is going to be fine. And then the second wave sank the boat. These people jumped to the right, towards the bank, whereas Vukasin went left, towards the centre of the river. The woman, she was hanging onto the fuel reservoir. Later on, they managed to get her out. She had passed out, but she was still clinging to that fuel reservoir.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You heard a version here, I mean, the one that was given by Borivoje Savic, that, in actual fact, it was some people who were divers and who had turned this boat over. Did you hear of that version from anyone else?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some leaders of opposition parties in Serbia were saying that too. That was the thesis of Milan Paroski. One cannot say that that is insane. It is 100 times crazier than insane.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, do you know what kind of relationship Borivoje Savic had with Soskocanin?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they knew each other, but Vukasin simply could not stand him, could not stand the sight of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know, for example, what Savic said? That's in his statement, P50, paragraph 73. That he gave Soskocanin a particular assignment to set up a group of 200 men to provide protection for members of the party.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's crazy. That is totally fabricated. It's a lie. Members of the party providing security for other members of the party? I mean, that is a totally insane idea. Well, Vukasin would never take any orders from Boro Savic. Vukasin was president of the local board of Borovo, and Boro Savic and I were not members of that board. We had nothing to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: May we move to the -- to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If you would please look at this document and tell us if this is the decision adopted at the Assembly session on 25 June 1991.

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at Article 1. Does it faithfully reflect what the Assembly decided; namely, that the people from Slavonia, Baranja, and Western Srem should remain within a single country along with the other parts populated by Serbs who wish the same thing?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And that is in keeping with what we have discussed today and the stance of Mr. De Michelis.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you recall if that Assembly session decided anything as to what the Serbian National Council should do in future? Did you get any tasks from the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember well, we were to monitor every step taken by Croatia. If the Croatia should continue to separate itself from Yugoslavia, within our mandate and as decided by the referendum, we should separate from Croatia, to remain within Yugoslavia. That's why the Assembly gave the mandate to the Serbian National Council to monitor these developments and to form a government that would eventually become -- to form a body that would eventually become the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you recall if you personally received an assignment from that Assembly? Were you entrusted with anything?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was to be the prime minister designate of that future government.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your understanding, what exactly were you supposed to do? What were your duties?

utterances.speaker: GORAN HADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this perspective, I could perhaps be able to explain it, but then, on the 25th of June, 1991, I was not quite sure what to expect and what my duties would be. We knew that we were to form an executive body that would represent those people who wished to remain in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think it's appropriate time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Mr. Hadzic, we adjourn for the day. You're still under oath, and you know what that means: You can't talk to anybody about your testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 8th day of July, 2014, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.59 p.m.,
